claims.text: stage-4: dev-secrets.sh writes encryption-config.yaml with a secretbox key of 32 random bytes (openssl rand -base64 32) as text, then identity, which only serves reads of data written unencrypted; encryption-at-rest.sh gives the file to the lab API server on the control-plane node.
claims.source_hint: scripts/dev-secrets.sh lines 86-106, scripts/k8s/encryption-at-rest.sh @ stage-4; Kubernetes docs encrypt-data > Providers (identity)

claims.text: On a managed cluster the provider usually runs the control plane, so the team has no node to put the EncryptionConfiguration file on and does not edit the API server's configuration.
claims.source_hint: k8s.l4.managed-control-plane outline 1; Kubernetes docs: Encrypting Confidential Data at Rest (config is an API server flag)

claims.text: The kms provider uses envelope encryption: resources are encrypted with a data encryption key (DEK); DEKs are encrypted by a key encryption key (KEK) stored and managed in a remote KMS; the encrypted DEK is stored in etcd alongside the ciphertext.
claims.source_hint: Kubernetes docs: Using a KMS provider for data encryption > KMS encryption and per-object encryption keys; Encrypting Confidential Data at Rest > Managed (KMS) key storage

claims.text: The API server encrypts the Secret's value itself with a data key; the value never goes to the KMS. Data keys are made from one random seed; the KMS encrypts the seed, and only the encrypted seed is stored beside the value. Decrypted data keys stay in memory; the KEK is never held.
claims.source_hint: Kubernetes docs: Using a KMS provider for data encryption (DEK/KEK, KMS v2 DEK from seed); Encrypting Confidential Data at Rest > Providers table (kms v2: data encrypted by DEKs using AES-GCM)

claims.text: The API server talks to the KMS through a KMS plugin, a server deployed on the same hosts as the control plane, which handles all communication with the remote KMS.
claims.source_hint: Kubernetes docs: Using a KMS provider for data encryption (KMS plugin gRPC server over a UNIX domain socket on control-plane hosts)

claims.text: KMS v2: once the API server has unwrapped a DEK via the KMS it caches it in the clear and can decrypt with it indefinitely without calling the KMS; so not every read calls the KMS, and reads of existing Secrets can continue during a short KMS outage.
claims.source_hint: Kubernetes docs: Using a KMS provider for data encryption > Configuring the KMS provider > KMS v2 (no cachesize; DEKs cached in the clear)

claims.text: If the KEK is disabled or deleted, the KMS stops decrypting: a running API server keeps reading with cached DEKs, but once it restarts, as it does after a snapshot is restored, no Secret encrypted under that key can be read.
claims.source_hint: Kubernetes docs: Encrypting Confidential Data at Rest > Managed (KMS) key storage (dependence on the KEK); KMS provider page (DEK cache in memory); ADR 0023 lines 37-41

claims.text: A copy of etcd or a snapshot holds ciphertext and encrypted DEKs but not the KEK, so reading needs the KMS (an attacker needs etcd and the KMS); credentials that let the API server call the KMS must themselves be protected.
claims.source_hint: Kubernetes docs: Encrypting Confidential Data at Rest > Managed (KMS) key storage; Protection for encryption keys

claims.text: 1.34: kms provider sits in the same EncryptionConfiguration providers list, apiVersion v2 (v1 off by default since 1.29); a kms entry names the plugin endpoint, holds no key. v2 derives DEKs from a seed the KMS encrypted and does not call EncryptRequest per Secret (not at a high rate).
claims.source_hint: Kubernetes docs: Using a KMS provider > KMS v2 (apiVersion, name, endpoint, timeout); KMS encryption and per-object encryption keys (DEK from seed); EncryptRequest rate

claims.text: A KMS keeps keys, often inside HSMs, and encrypts, decrypts or signs on request for permitted callers, recording each use (ADR 0023 context: the key never leaves the HSM, permitted callers send data to sign and get the signature, each use logged).
claims.source_hint: docs/adr/0023-khoa-ky-hoa-don-trong-hsm-cua-nha-cung-cap.md lines 12-14 @ stage-4; Kubernetes docs encrypt-data (kms implementations can work with HSMs)

claims.text: Opinion: hosting providers that run the API server usually supply their own KMS plugin for their key service; turning it on follows the provider's instructions, not the EncryptionConfiguration file.
claims.source_hint: Kubernetes docs: Using a KMS provider > Enabling the KMS supported by your cloud provider; ADR 0023 lines 37-39

claims.text: ADR 0023 options @ stage-4: own HSM needs devices in two places and people to run, upgrade, back up (the work ADR 0022 declined for the cluster); provider's HSM service: no hardware, tied to provider; software key in KMS: cheapest, fails ADR 0015's HSM requirement.
claims.source_hint: docs/adr/0023-khoa-ky-hoa-don-trong-hsm-cua-nha-cung-cap.md lines 18-24 @ stage-4

claims.text: ADR 0023 decision: provider's HSM service; only Payments' ServiceAccount may sign, nobody else incl. the team lead; key administration (create, disable) is a separate right.
claims.source_hint: docs/adr/0023-khoa-ky-hoa-don-trong-hsm-cua-nha-cung-cap.md lines 26-30 @ stage-4

claims.text: ADR 0023 consequences: key cannot leave the HSM, so leaving means a new key and certificate; old invoices stay verifiable with public key and certificate. Production Secrets use a key of the same KMS (envelope encryption) instead of the lab secretbox file; disable/delete rights guarded like data.
claims.source_hint: docs/adr/0023-khoa-ky-hoa-don-trong-hsm-cua-nha-cung-cap.md lines 34-41 @ stage-4

claims.text: Verifying a digital signature needs only the public key (and the certificate binding it), not the private key.
claims.source_hint: glossary digital-signature, public-key; backend.l4.pki-and-signing; ADR 0015 lines 10-13, 47-49

claims.text: ADR 0023 reopening: a contract requiring the key in an HSM on Đơn Hàng's or a customer's own machines leads to a new ADR for that key only, other keys unchanged. Each signing is logged by the KMS besides audit-log.md.
claims.source_hint: docs/adr/0023-khoa-ky-hoa-don-trong-hsm-cua-nha-cung-cap.md lines 42-49 @ stage-4

claims.text: ADR 0015: a compromised Payments can request signatures only while the compromise lasts and cannot carry the key off; after the fix no new signature is made with that key.
claims.source_hint: docs/adr/0015-khoa-ky-hoa-don-trong-hsm.md lines 35-37, 54 @ stage-4

claims.text: Opinion (trade-offs and choices): keep the secretbox file for the lab when no key service exists, since a local key still protects snapshots taken off the node; refuse 'emergency' signing rights because ADR 0023 separates signing from key administration.
claims.source_hint: k8s.l3.encryption-at-rest (local key protects snapshots); ADR 0023 lines 28-30; Kubernetes docs encrypt-data > Local key storage

claims.text: A local secretbox key in the EncryptionConfiguration on the host protects against an etcd compromise but not a host compromise: a copy of the node's disk holds both.
claims.source_hint: Kubernetes docs: Encrypting Confidential Data at Rest > Key storage > Local key storage

claims.text: Lab encryption config lists only secrets under resources, so a snapshot of the lab cluster with encryption at rest keeps ConfigMaps and other objects readable; only Secrets written after encryption was turned on are encrypted (earlier ones stay under identity until rewritten).
claims.source_hint: scripts/dev-secrets.sh lines 91-106 @ stage-4; Kubernetes docs encrypt-data > Ensure all Secrets are encrypted; Providers (identity)
